newsitem.title: USA: The economy - Too slow too soon?.
newsitem.headline: The economy - Too slow too soon?.

text.p: With the Dow industrials within a hair's breadth of 6,000, the S&P 500 passing a milestone and long-term interest rates apparently headed lower, the outlook for stocks has suddenly turned cautious.

Friday's shockingly weak employment report, which saw U.S. payrolls decline by 40,000, convinced many economists the Federal Reserve would refrain from raising interest rates at its November meeting and sent the bond market soaring.

Stocks followed suit, with the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks topping the 700-point level for the first time to finish at 701.46. The index has scored record closes four times this week, ending up 15.27 from last Friday.
The Dow Jones industrial average rallied 60.01 points to end at 5,992.86, topping Wednesday's record close of 5,933.97. For the week, the blue chip index was up 119.94 points or 2 percent.
Likewise, the NYSE Composite index, which scored a record every day this week except for Thursday, rose 4.02 to 374.16, an all-time high finish. The index was up 7.89 on the week.
The technology-studded Nasdaq Composite index soared 14.47 points, or 1.17 percent, to 1,247.56, just shy of June 5's record 1,249.15. The index was up 17.51 on the week.
Market analysts were nearly unanimous, however, in warning that on this occasion, what was good news for the bond market represented a mixed blessing, at best, for stocks.

"The issue is, does the payrolls number really equate to a slowing down in the third quarter and does that mean that corporate earnings will be lower?" said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
"Whether we go through 6,000 or back to 5,500 is going to depend on earnings," he added.
The renewed focus on profits is partly a function of the reporting cycle. Quarterly reporting is slated to begin in earnest next week, with banks traditionally first to file.

While Wall Street clearly favours low interest rates, the manner in which this is happening -- an economy that seems suddenly to be slowing more quickly than expected -- is less than ideal for stocks.

"You can't get away from the possibility that in a slowing economy, earnings will also slow," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "I'm a little worried that the market may be forecasting stronger third-quarter earnings than are possible."
The fact that stocks were able to participate in Friday's rally failed to convince analysts that the apparently tamer inflation outlook would fuel a sustained stock rally.

"There are two kinds of markets, ones that anticipate and ones that react," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Friday's move was reactive and usually gains that are reactive are not as powerful."
One indication companies may be bracing for a downturn may be the shrinking rate of dividend increases.

According to Standard & Poor's Outlook, an investment advisory news letter, September marked the second straight month of year-to-year declines in the number of dividend increases reported to Standard & Poor's.
"The slowdown in dividend increases may mean that companies are conserving cash out of fear that profits will level off in 1997," Outlook editor Arnold Kaufman said.
Among the Dow industrials, AT&T Corp. and Aluminum Co. of America have already warned about or reported disappointing earnings.
While caution flags have been raised on the market, analysts stopped short of calling for a sell-off like July's.

"This market has had a huge run since the July lows so I would not disagree that it would level off here," Cripps said. "But I don't think we'll go much lower unless people get disillusioned with stocks."
Bonds remain an uninspiring alternative, analysts said, precisely because yields have worked their way so low.

Another sign of mounting earnings concern was that the worries have all but eclipsed the presidential election as a topic of interest on Wall Street, perhaps in part because many view the outcome of the election as a foregone conclusion.

As such, somewhat less attention is being paid to topics like which sectors might thrive under which candidate. However, analysts cited one sector that could serve as a barometer for the Dole campaign's prospects.
"If you want to know how well Bob Dole did in the debate on Sunday, look at the tobacco stocks on Monday," said Froehlich.
